summary: Adds a new Abuse Reporting Format feedback type, "not-spam", which can be used to report an email message that was wrongly marked as spam. It is a small standards-track extension.

eli5.summary: Sometimes a good letter gets thrown in the junk pile by mistake. This gives a standard way to tell the mail system "that one was fine".

questions: how to report a false positive spam message
what is the arf not-spam feedback type
how to report a message wrongly marked as spam
what is the abuse reporting format
subtitle: A new feedback report type that lets a mail user say a message was wrongly marked as spam.

tldr.problem: The Abuse Reporting Format had report types for abuse and fraud, but no standard way to tell an email operator that a message was mistakenly marked as spam.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6430 defines a new feedback report type value, "not-spam", for use in the existing report format of RFC 5965. The user or client can add a note in the first MIME part explaining why the message is not spam.
tldr.outcome: Operators get a standard signal to weigh alongside other data, not an automatic override. It was registered with IANA as a current feedback type.

today: RFC 6430 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 5965.

sections.title: A Report for Mistaken Spam Marks
sections.content:
RFC 5965 defines the Abuse Reporting Format (ARF) for reporting email abuse. Two report types related to spam already exist: abuse for unsolicited email or other abuse, and fraud for fraud or phishing activity.

This RFC adds a third, not-spam. It is used to report a message that was mistakenly marked as spam.
sections.eli5: There was already a way to say a letter was junk. Now there is also a way to say a letter was marked junk by mistake.

sections.title: Why Operators Want These Reports
sections.content:
A message can be wrongly tagged as spam by the email system, or accidentally by the user. The email client takes the user's "not-spam" instruction, gathers information about the message, and reports it to the email operator. The need for the report type came from the Open Mobile Alliance spam report requirements.

The operator decides what to do. It could remove the spam tag or reclassify the message, which may keep similar mail for that user from being marked as spam later. It could also use the report to adjust the training of an automated classifier, or notify the client of the result, for example by moving the message from "Junk" to "Inbox".
sections.eli5: If the mail helper put your letter in the junk pile by mistake, you tell it, and it can learn and maybe move the letter back.

sections.title: The not-spam Report Type
sections.content:
The new value, not-spam, extends the Email Feedback Reports specification in RFC 5965. The report is an ordinary feedback report whose Feedback-Type field is not-spam.

In the first MIME part of the report message, the end user or the email client can add text saying why the message is not considered spam, for example because the originator or its domain is well known.
sections.eli5: The note on the front of the report can say why the letter is fine, like "I know this sender".

sections.title: An Example Report
sections.content:
The RFC's example follows Joe, a pharmaceuticals sales representative. A message about discount pharmaceuticals, a frequent subject of spam, was marked as spam incorrectly. Joe reports it as not-spam.

The report is a multipart/report message with report-type=feedback-report. Its first part is a human-readable text with Joe's comment, the second is a message/feedback-report part carrying Feedback-Type: not-spam, User-Agent and Version: 1, and the third is the original message. The report is signed with DKIM, which the RFC calls a good security practice as suggested in Section 8.2 of RFC 5965.
sections.eli5: Joe sells medicine, so a message about medicine discounts is normal for him. He sends back a form saying it is not junk, with the original letter attached.

sections.title: How Operators Should Treat Reports
sections.content:
The RFC expects that "not-spam" reports will usually not be acted on alone, but considered together with other information and analysis of the message. Different users have different views of what is spam, so one user's report may not apply to others. Users may also press a "report not spam" button by accident, so immediate strong action, such as marking all similar messages as good from a single report, is probably not the right approach.

Existing anti-spam systems already use non-standard "not spam" feedback. They mix it with other reports and data, and none uses it as an immediate, automatic override. The types abuse and not-spam can be seen as opposites, so a mistaken not-spam report could be countermanded by a later abuse report from the same user.
sections.eli5: One person saying "this is fine" is a hint, not an order. The mail helper should check other clues before changing its mind.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All security considerations from RFC 5965 are inherited. The Applicability Statement for ARF (a Work in Progress at the time) adds information about trust relationships and the integrity of accepting abuse feedback.

The RFC points out that not-spam reports will likely be used in attacks on a filtering system, by reporting true spam as "not-spam". Even without malice, some reports will be made in error or apply only to the sender of the report. Operators need to be careful about trusting such reports beyond their applicability to the specific user.
sections.eli5: A sneaky person could say real junk is fine to trick the filter, so the helper must not just believe every report.
